MUQATIL:102:1-7/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:102:1-7/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:102:1-7/r4.claim: The rivalry continued until all of them came to the graves.

FARRA:v3p287/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p287/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p287/r1.claim: Two Quraysh clans, Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū Sahm, competed in counting the living and then the dead to prove which had more people.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p538#3/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p538#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p538#3/r1.claim: They continued counting the dead buried in the graves.

TAB-FULL:v24p598#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p598#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p598#2/r1.claim: People are distracted from obeying their Lord and seeking deliverance from His anger by competing and boasting about abundance of wealth and numbers.

TAB-FULL:v24p598#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p598#2/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p598#2/r2.claim: Qatadah describes tribes boasting that they outnumber other tribes until every generation falls away and all become people of the graves; this rivalry distracted them until they died astray.

TAB-FULL:v24p598#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p598#2/r3.speaker: النبي
TAB-FULL:v24p598#2/r3.claim: After reciting the verse, the Prophet says a person's wealth is only what he consumes, wears out, or gives in charity and sends ahead.

TAB-FULL:v24p598#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p598#2/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p598#2/r5.claim: The Prophet's comment after reciting the surah confirms that the abundance distracting people is wealth.

TAB-FULL:v24p600/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p600/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p600/r1.claim: Visiting the graves means dying and being buried there; the verse threatens them with what they will encounter after burial and supports the reality of punishment in the grave.

ZAJJAJ:v5p357/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p357/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p357/r2.claim: Visiting the graves means death caught them in that state.

NAHHAS:v5p283/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p283/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p283/r1.claim: The best sense is that rivalry in abundance distracted people from obedience until burial; this verse indicates punishment in the grave.

NAHHAS:v5p283/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p283/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p283/r2.claim: Visiting the graves means reaching the burial grounds.

NAHHAS:v5p283/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p283/r3.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
NAHHAS:v5p283/r3.claim: A report from Zirr says the chapter was revealed about punishment in the grave and was recited through ‘No indeed, you will know.’

NAHHAS:v5p283/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p283/r4.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v5p283/r4.claim: He gives maqbara and maqbara as singular forms; some Hijazis use a different vowel, as in variants of mashriqa.

THALABI:v10p276#3/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p276#3/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p276#3/r2.claim: Visiting the graves means dying and being buried in them.

THALABI:v10p276#3/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p276#3/r3.speaker: قتادة
THALABI:v10p276#3/r3.claim: He says the surah came down about Jews comparing which clan was larger, a contest that distracted them until they died astray.

THALABI:v10p276#3/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p276#3/r4.speaker: ابن بريدة
THALABI:v10p276#3/r4.claim: He says it came down about a clan among the Ansar who boasted against one another.

THALABI:v10p276#3/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p276#3/r5.speaker: مقاتل والكلبي
THALABI:v10p276#3/r5.claim: They say two Quraysh clans disputed which had more leaders and numbers, then counted their dead in graves; Banu Sahm outnumbered Banu Abd Manaf by three households, prompting the revelation.

THALABI:v10p276#3/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p276#3/r7.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
THALABI:v10p276#3/r7.claim: He says Muslims remained unsure about punishment in the grave until ‘you will know’ was revealed, referring to the grave.

THALABI:v10p281/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p281/r4.speaker: النبي
THALABI:v10p281/r4.claim: In Ibn Abbas’s report, takathur is wrongful accumulation and withholding; the passage follows people through graves and judgment, then names five blessings: full stomach, cold drink, sleep, shade, and sound constitution.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p330/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p330/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p330/r5.claim: One reading is that death brings people to the graves as visitors, from which they return to their lasting home in Paradise or Hell.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p330/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p330/r6.speaker: الكلبي، قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p330/r6.claim: Al-Kalbi and Qatada report that two Quraysh clans, Abd Manaf and Sahm, competed over numbers; when Sahm counted the dead as well as the living and surpassed the others, the verse was revealed about counting the dead in graves.

QUSHAYRI:v3p445/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p445/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p445/r3.claim: People's mutual boasting occupied them through the end of their lives, until they died.

QUSHAYRI:v3p445/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p445/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p445/r4.claim: Another interpretation is that they boasted of their forefathers and ancestors, celebrating the living and those who had died.

QUSHAYRI:v3p445/r5.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p445/r5.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p445/r5.claim: Their boasting led them to count their dead as they counted the living, and their competition in wealth and children distracted them from obedience to God.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p464/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p464/r1.speaker: مقاتل والكلبي
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p464/r1.claim: Muqātil and al-Kalbī say the passage concerns Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū Sahm competing over which clan had more notables, then counting their dead at the graves; Banū Sahm had more.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p464/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p464/r2.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p464/r2.claim: Qatāda offers another view: the verse concerns Jews boasting that one group outnumbered another until death carried them off in error.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r1.claim: The phrase means that death overtook people while they were still occupied with rivalry.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r2.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r2.claim: Qatada says it was revealed about Jews who boasted that their clans outnumbered other clans, distracting them from faith until they died astray.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r3.claim: The warning includes everyone who lets boasting and rivalry distract from obedience until death.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r4.speaker: النبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r4.claim: The Prophet says a person's lasting wealth is only what was eaten, worn, or given away in charity.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r5.speaker: صاحب النظم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r5.claim: The author of al-Nazm says people continue competing and boasting until death.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r6.speaker: جرير
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r6.claim: Jarir's poetry shows that saying someone visited graves can mean that the person died.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r7.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل وابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r7.claim: Al-Kalbi, Muqatil, and Ibn Abbas (through Ata) say the verse concerns Quraysh clans Banu Abd Manaf and Banu Sahm, who counted the dead in their graveyards while boasting; Banu Sahm were more numerous.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r8.speaker: ابن بريدة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r8.claim: Ibn Burayda says it concerned an Ansar clan boasting about its forefathers and naming their graves.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p276#2/r9.claim: On the clan-boasting interpretation, they went to the graves and mentioned their dead relatives while competing.

WAHIDI-QT:102:1/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:102:1/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:102:1/r2.claim: The competition continued until death overtook them in that state.

WAHIDI-QT:102:1/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:102:1/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:102:1/r3.claim: The passage was revealed about Jews who boasted that their clans outnumbered others and died astray while distracted from faith.

WAHIDI-QT:102:2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:102:2/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:102:2/r2.claim: The competition continued until death overtook them in that state.

WAHIDI-QT:102:2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:102:2/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:102:2/r3.claim: The passage was revealed about Jews who boasted that their clans outnumbered others and died astray while distracted from faith.

JISHUMI:v10p7523/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7523/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7523/r7.claim: A visit is going to a place as one goes to water, without remaining there; zūr can also mean a false imitation of handwriting.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p515#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p515#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p515#2/r2.claim: Visiting the graves means dying and being buried in them.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p515#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p515#2/r3.speaker: قتادة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p515#2/r3.claim: Qatada says the passage concerns Jews boasting that they outnumbered one another; the rivalry distracted them until they died astray.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p515#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p515#2/r4.speaker: مقاتل والكلبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p515#2/r4.claim: They say two Quraysh clans, Banu Abd Manaf and Banu Sahm, competed over noblemen and numbers, then counted their dead in graves; Banu Sahm claimed more because they had been more numerous in pre-Islamic times.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p515#2/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p515#2/r6.speaker: أنس بن مالك عن رسول الله
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p515#2/r6.claim: Anas reports the Prophet's saying that three follow the dead, but family and wealth return while the person's deeds remain.

KASHSHAF:102:2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:102:2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:102:2/r1.claim: One view says people visited graves while boasting, pointing out whose grave was whose.

KASHSHAF:102:2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:102:2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:102:2/r2.claim: Their rivalry distracted them with something useless in this life and the next, away from the more important work of religion.

KASHSHAF:102:2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:102:2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:102:2/r3.claim: Alternatively, pursuit and rivalry over wealth and children consume life until death and burial, diverting people from preparing for the next life; visiting graves is a metaphor for death.

KASHSHAF:102:2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:102:2/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:102:2/r4.claim: The first cited poem uses visiting the grave as the endpoint of a year, supporting the metaphor of death.

KASHSHAF:102:2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:102:2/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:102:2/r5.claim: A second poetic line about Abu Malik visiting graves likewise illustrates grave-visiting as death.

KASHSHAF:102:2/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:102:2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
KASHSHAF:102:2/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas reads the opening with an interrogative hamza, whose question serves to assert the rebuke.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p518#3/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p518#3/r6.speaker: قوم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p518#3/r6.claim: Some say people boast about dead ancestors and their bones until death overtakes them.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p518#3/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p518#3/r7.speaker: قوم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p518#3/r7.claim: Others take visiting graves as dying and entering one's grave after spending one's life in rivalry; a Bedouin inferred resurrection, and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz is credited with the view.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p518#3/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p518#3/r8.speaker: آخرون
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p518#3/r8.claim: Others condemn excessive grave visiting to boast in forebears, distracting from worship and learning.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p518#3/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p518#3/r9.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p518#3/r9.claim: The Prophet first forbade grave visits, then permitted visits for reflection, not boasting and lavish decoration.

TABRISI:102:1-7/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:102:1-7/r5.speaker: الحسن
TABRISI:102:1-7/r5.claim: Visiting the graves means death overtook people in their rivalry; al-Hasan and Qatada say they died without repenting.

TABRISI:102:1-7/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:102:1-7/r6.speaker: الجبائي
TABRISI:102:1-7/r6.claim: The phrase may mean they died still in that condition without repentance.

TABRISI:102:1-7/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:102:1-7/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:102:1-7/r7.claim: Another explanation says rivalry in wealth and numbers distracted them from reflecting on God's command until they counted the dead in graves.

RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r2.claim: The wording حتى زرتم المقابر sounds like a completed event; the verse mocks the thought that merely outnumbering rivals has any benefit.

RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r3.claim: A report urges grave visits because they remind people of death; here the rivals visited graves because of hard hearts and immersion in worldly love.

RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r5.claim: On the wealth reading, visiting graves is a metaphor for dying; Jarir's line uses visiting graves to mean Abu Malik died.

RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r6.claim: Al-Razi raises two objections: visitors leave while the dead remain, and the past-tense wording seems incompatible with future death.

RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p73#2/r7.claim: Replies say the dead too must leave for judgment; the address may concern people near death, earlier generations on whose path the living follow, or disbelievers on Judgment Day after their graves are visited.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r10.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن ابن مسعود
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r10.claim: The Prophet first forbade grave visits, then permitted them because they make people renounce the world and remember the afterlife; Ibn Mas'ud's report is in Ibn Majah.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r5.claim: Visiting graves means death: people become visitors to their graves and return from them to their final home in Paradise or Hell.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r6.claim: Another interpretation says boasting lasted until people counted the dead; another treats the verse as a warning about seeing God's punishment in the graves.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r7.claim: Maqabir is the plural of maqbara in either vowelled form; qubur is the plural of qabr, with additional poetic and lexical forms.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r8.claim: The paired verb forms distinguish burying someone from ordering that person buried; Qurtubi notes that the issue was discussed in Surah Abasa.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#2/r9.claim: This is the Qur'an's only mention of graves; visiting them is a powerful cure for a hard heart because it recalls death and the afterlife, shortening worldly hopes.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r1.claim: The continuation of the Muslim report says grave visits remind people of death.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r2.speaker: بريدة
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r2.claim: Al-Tirmidhi transmits from Burayda that grave visits remind people of the afterlife and grades the report Hasan Sahih.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r3.speaker: أبو هريرة
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r3.claim: A report in al-Tirmidhi says the Prophet cursed women who frequently visit graves; the chapter also cites Ibn Abbas and Hassan ibn Thabit.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r4.speaker: أبو عيسى
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r4.claim: Abu Isa grades the report about women who frequently visit graves Hasan Sahih.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r5.speaker: بعض أهل العلم
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r5.claim: Some scholars say the curse came before the Prophet later permitted grave visits, after which the permission included women as well as men.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r6.speaker: بعضهم
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r6.claim: Others restrict the disapproval to women because they are thought to have less patience and greater grief.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r7.claim: Men's grave visits are agreed upon, while women's visits are disputed; Qurtubi permits older women and allows women to go when separated from men.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#3/r8.claim: Where a mixed gathering risks temptation, visits are unlawful: either sex may be distracted by the other's presence and leave sinful rather than rewarded.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#4/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#4/r2.claim: The report transmitted by Ibn Abbas says direct experience is not like hearing about an event.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#4/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#4/r3.claim: A visitor should attend with a present heart, seeking God, repairing the heart, or benefiting the dead with Qur'an and prayer; merely touring graves is an animal-like activity.

QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#4/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:102:1-2#4/r4.claim: Visitors should avoid walking or sitting on graves, greet the cemetery and the known deceased, and face the deceased as they would a living person they address.

BAYDAWI-FULL:102:1-2/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:102:1-2/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:102:1-2/r2.claim: After counting the living, people reach the graves and boast of their dead; a report describes Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū Sahm successively claiming more living and dead, with omitted religious concerns intensifying the rebuke.

BAYDAWI-FULL:102:1-2/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:102:1-2/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:102:1-2/r3.claim: Alternatively, worldly competition in wealth and children distracts people until death and burial; visiting graves is a metaphor for dying.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p354#13/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p354#13/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p354#13/r1.claim: One interpretation is that death overtook people while they were still distracted by rivalry.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p354#13/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p354#13/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p354#13/r2.claim: Alternatively, they visited graves and counted the dead among their people.

QASHANI:102:1-4/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:102:1-4/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:102:1-4/r2.claim: Competition over wealth, children, and ancestry can extend even to boasting about long-dead ancestors’ bones, driven by imagination and concealing illusion.

QASHANI:102:1-4/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:102:1-4/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:102:1-4/r3.claim: Alternatively, the rivalry continues until death: people spend their whole lives in it and never notice what would save them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r1.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r1.claim: The surah is Meccan according to all exegetes, while al-Bukhārī calls it Madinan.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r10.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r10.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya criticizes people who embellish and raise graves with stone and marble; Abū Ḥayyān replies that he had not seen the lavish Egyptian cemeteries and their wasted wealth.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r2.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r2.claim: Al-Kalbī and Muqātil say the rival clans of Sahm and ʿAbd Manāf counted their living notables, then their dead; ʿAbd Manāf had more living, but Sahm more dead from pre-Islamic times.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r3.speaker: قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r3.claim: Qatada says the passage concerns Jews who claimed their tribes outnumbered other tribes.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r4.speaker: ابن زيد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r4.claim: Ibn Zayd says it concerns a clan among the Anṣār.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r6.claim: The author calls the use of visiting graves for counting the dead a sarcastic metaphor that poorly fits the ordinary sense of visiting; another reading is that rivalry consumed life until death.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r7.claim: An Arab and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz understood the wording literally: visitors leave rather than remain, so the people must be raised again.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r8.claim: Another interpretation is that they repeatedly visited graves to outdo one another in honoring and remembering the dead.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r9.speaker: الرسول
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p535/r9.claim: The Prophet first prohibited grave visits, then allowed them for taking admonition rather than boasting and rivalry.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p536/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p536/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p536/r1.claim: The author criticizes devotees who boast of visiting saints' tombs, preserve lengthy shrine stories without knowing purification duties, and exploit popular generosity for money and status.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p536/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p536/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p536/r2.claim: He adds that people with some learning imitate the popular shrine storytellers to gain wealth, prestige, and hand-kissing, and prays for God's guidance to obedience.

SAMIN-DURR:102:2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:102:2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:102:2/r1.claim: ‘Hatta’ marks the endpoint of ‘alhakum’ and is coordinated with that verb.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p472#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p472#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p472#2/r1.claim: Love of worldly life, its pleasures, and its adornments distracts people from seeking the afterlife until death brings them to the graves.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p472#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p472#2/r2.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p472#2/r2.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet says rivalry distracted people from obedience until death came; Ibn Kathīr gives no grading here.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p472#2/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p472#2/r7.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p472#2/r7.claim: The dead person is followed by family, wealth, and deeds; family and wealth return, while deeds remain.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p473/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p473/r4.speaker: ابن بريدة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p473/r4.claim: Ibn Burayda reports that the sūra was revealed about Banū Ḥāritha and Banū al-Ḥārith boasting over living and dead members of their tribes at the graves.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p473/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p473/r5.speaker: قتادة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p473/r5.claim: Qatāda says people boasted that their tribe was more numerous than another, while their members kept dying until all became grave-dwellers.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p473/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p473/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p473/r6.claim: Ibn Kathīr prefers that visiting the graves means reaching them and being buried there, citing the Prophet's reply to a sick man who said fever would send him to the graves.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p473/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p473/r7.speaker: علي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p473/r7.claim: ʿAlī reports that the Muslims continued to doubt punishment in the grave until this sūra was revealed; Ibn Kathīr later cites al-Tirmidhī calling the report gharīb.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p474/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p474/r1.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p474/r1.claim: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz reflects that graves are only a visit, and a visitor must return to a home; Ibn Kathīr explains the destination as Paradise or Hell.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p474/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p474/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p474/r2.claim: Ibn Kathīr explains ʿUmar's “home” as the person's eventual home in Paradise or Hell.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p474/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p474/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p474/r3.claim: An unnamed Bedouin hears “until you visit the graves” and declares that the Resurrection has happened today, since a visitor will leave that place for another.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p516#2/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p516#2/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p516#2/r4.claim: Calling burial a visit signals that life in the grave is temporary and resurrection certain: the dead cannot act there, and will return to permanent Paradise or Hell.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p516#2/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p516#2/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p516#2/r5.claim: Death alone should deter people from worldly absorption, since it is the first stage of their being presented for judgment.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p516#2/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p516#2/r6.speaker: أبو حيان
BIQAI-FULL:v8p516#2/r6.claim: Abū Ḥayyān reports that a Bedouin, hearing the verse, concluded that people will be raised, since a visitor leaves rather than staying forever.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p516#2/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p516#2/r7.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
BIQAI-FULL:v8p516#2/r7.claim: Ibn Abī al-Dunyā reports that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said graves are only a visit and the visitor must return either to Paradise or to Hell.

DURR-FULL:v8p610/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p610/r6.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
DURR-FULL:v8p610/r6.claim: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz reads the verse without the conjunction and says graves are only a visit, so visitors must return home.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p234#2/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p234#2/r1.speaker: ابن بريدة
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p234#2/r1.claim: Ibn Burayda reports that the Ansar tribes Banu Haritha and Banu al-Harith competed by boasting about their living members, then went to the graves and boasted of the dead; the surah was revealed.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p234#2/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p234#2/r2.speaker: علي
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p234#2/r2.claim: Ali reports that the Muslims doubted punishment in the grave until the passage from “competition distracts you” through “then you will know” was revealed regarding that punishment.

BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r1.speaker: الكاشفي
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r1.claim: Al-Kashifi says the tribes went to the cemetery and counted the graves of their own notables to compare numbers.

BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r2.claim: They continued competing until they counted the dead and boasted in their dead; visiting graves is a euphemism for mentioning the dead and a sarcastic inversion of the visit's purpose.

BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r3.speaker: الطيبي
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r3.claim: Al-Tibi says grave visitation was legislated to recall death, renounce love of worldly life, and abandon boasting; these people instead made it a cause of hardness and deeper worldly attachment.

BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r4.claim: The verse is a declarative rebuke, and on this reading the endpoint “until” is included in the distraction.

BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r5.claim: Another reading says worldly competition in wealth and children distracted them until they died and were buried; grave visitation then means death after wasted lives and neglect of the afterlife.

BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r6.speaker: رسول الله
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r6.claim: The Prophet says a person owns only what he consumed, wore out, or gave in charity from his wealth.

BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r7.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r7.claim: ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz says graves are a place one visits and must leave, returning either to Paradise or the Fire.

BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r8.claim: Because a visitor departs rather than staying, the wording hints at resurrection and warns against worldly life while urging preparation for death and the afterlife.

BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p387#2/r9.claim: A Persian poem warns that death will raid and one must leave the world; an unenslaved heart travels to the next world with ease.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r1.claim: The people counted all the living, then turned to the graves and counted their dead; the endpoint is included in the distraction, and the occasion of revelation explains the image.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r10.speaker: جرير
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r10.claim: Jarir likewise uses grave visitation for death, saying Abu Malik visited the graves and became their most ignoble visitor.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r11.claim: The expression points to resurrection; an Arab reportedly inferred that the people must be raised for Judgment, since a visitor departs rather than remains.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r12.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r12.claim: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz says every visitor must return to either Paradise or Hell, also suggesting a short stay in the graves.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r13.claim: The past tense indicates certainty, the predominance of those who died first, or treating the deaths of ancestors as their own.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r14.speaker: أبو مسلم
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r14.claim: Abu Muslim says God will reproach the disbelievers with this surah on Judgment Day, after they have visited graves; the author calls this astonishing.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r15.speaker: قيل
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r15.claim: A different interpretation rebukes excessive grave-visiting done to boast about predecessors; the author says the verse is far from that meaning and instead affirms visits for remembering the Hereafter.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r16.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r16.claim: The author condemns boasting over graves and the associated abuses of some ignorant Sufis, while recognizing grave-visiting for admonition as prescribed.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r2.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r2.claim: Banu Abd Manaf and Banu Sahm competed in numbers; after Abd Manaf first prevailed, Sahm counted the dead too and claimed victory.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r3.claim: In the reported contest, visiting graves means reaching the point of mentioning the dead, figuratively or by metonymy; the author favors treating it as a representation.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r4.speaker: الكشاف
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r4.claim: Al-Kashshaf reads the grave-visiting expression as mockery of the competitors.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r5.speaker: بعض
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r5.claim: One explanation of the mockery likens them to someone visiting graves without a sound purpose.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r6.speaker: بعض آخر
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r6.claim: Another explanation, which the author prefers, says grave visits should prompt reflection on death, but these people turned them into a cause of heedlessness.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r7.claim: The rivalry distracted people from the religious duty that truly matters; omitting the object of distraction magnifies the reproach through ambiguity and emphasizes the blame.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r8.claim: An alternative reading says wealth and children distracted people until death and burial; Ibn Abbas is cited for this interpretation, with al-Hasan also reported by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Abi Shayba.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r9.speaker: الشاعر
ALUSI-FULL:v30p223#3/r9.claim: Poetry uses visiting the grave as an expression for dying, supporting the interpretation of grave visitation as death.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r10.speaker: Katâde
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r10.claim: Qatada says rival clans claimed superiority and seniority while their people kept dying until all became inhabitants of graves.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r11.claim: The verse's apparent sense best suits numerical boasting; other vain rivalries are implied, and the following kalla rebukes them.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r12.claim: A second reading says desire for wealth, children, and numbers consumed the whole lifespan until death, leaving no effort for the afterlife; Ahtal and Jarir use grave-visiting for death.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r13.speaker: Ahtal
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r13.claim: Ahtal's verse uses visiting a grave as an expression for dying.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r14.speaker: Cerîr
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r14.claim: Jarir likewise says Abu Malik visited the graves, meaning he died.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r15.speaker: Alî
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r15.claim: Ali reports that they remained uncertain about grave punishment until this surah was revealed, yielding the sense until you taste the punishment of the grave.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r16.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r16.claim: On the grave-punishment reading, worldly hoarders awaken when they enter the grave, leaving transient possessions but carrying their burden; in both death readings takathur ends at burial.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r17.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r17.claim: The past form zurتم can convey a certain future, include those already dead, depict dying groups, or be construed as a time phrase meaning until the visit.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r18.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r18.speaker: Ebû Müslim
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r18.claim: Abu Muslim says God will address unbelievers with this surah on Resurrection Day, but the next clause about certain knowledge fits an address in this world or the grave better.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r19.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r19.speaker: A‘râbî
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r19.claim: An Arab listener swore that the people would be raised for judgment because a visitor departs rather than remaining at the visited place.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r20.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r20.speaker: Ömer b. Abdülaziz
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r20.claim: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz says every visitor must leave for either Paradise or Hell, and the image also suggests the dead do not remain long in graves.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r7.claim: The first interpretation, tied to the tribal reports, is that people were distracted into counting and boasting of the dead; grave visits should instead awaken reflection and prompt deeds that weigh heavily.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r8.speaker: Keşşâf
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r8.claim: On the first report, visiting graves is a metaphor or metonymy for boasting by counting the dead; Kashshaf prefers this reading.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#2/r9.claim: A second interpretation takes the visits literally, following the report in which the groups actually went to the graves.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r1.claim: The endpoint clause may attach to takathur or ilhā: people multiplied until visiting graves, were distracted into grave-boasting, or stayed distracted until death or grave-punishment.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r10.claim: People misuse grave visits when they boast in ancestors without inheriting their virtues, hold displays over graves, waste money for show, and ignore hungry neighbors; such conduct falls under the rebuke.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r11.speaker: Dürr-i Muhtâr
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r11.claim: The juristic manual says visiting graves is unobjectionable even for women, citing the prophetic instruction to visit.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r12.speaker: İmdâd, Müctebâ, Bahr ve Redd-i Muhtâr
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r12.claim: These manuals say grave-visiting is recommended because the hadith commands it.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r13.speaker: Redd-i Muhtâr
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r13.claim: Radd al-Muhtar recommends weekly visits and lists Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday, and Thursday as preferred days.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r14.speaker: Fethu’l-Kadîr
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r14.claim: Fath al-Qadir says the established Sunnah during a grave visit is prayer, following the Prophet's practice at Baqi and his greeting to the believers.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r15.speaker: Şerh-i Lübâb
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r15.claim: The visitor should approach from the feet rather than the head when possible; reports also place the Prophet at the head of one deceased person and the feet of another while reading Baqara.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r16.speaker: Şerh-i Lübâb
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r16.claim: Adab includes greeting with assalamu alaykum, standing for supplication, sitting according to the deceased's former status if needed, and reciting whatever Quran is easy, including the listed surahs and repeated Ikhlas.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r17.speaker: İbn Âbidîn
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r17.claim: Ibn Abidin details the dedication of recitation and other acts' rewards to the deceased; the jurists allow transferring rewards from prayer, fasting, charity, and other deeds.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r18.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r18.speaker: Tatarhâniyye
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r18.claim: The best practice is to intend one's charity for all believing men and women, since its reward reaches them without reducing one's own.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r19.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r19.speaker: Hafız İbn Teymiyye
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r19.claim: Ibn Taymiyya wished to forbid dedicating Quran recitation's reward to the Prophet, arguing that it requires his specific permission and that one should instead send blessings and ask for wasila.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r2.claim: The surface reading favors the first reports, where the endpoint is included and grave-visiting marks the maximum of blameworthy boasting; the rebuke is limited to visits for rivalry.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r20.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r20.speaker: Sübkî ve daha diğerleri
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r20.claim: Subki and others reject Ibn Taymiyya's restriction, arguing that no specific permission is needed and citing Ibn Umar and others.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r3.claim: The verse leaves other motives outside its explicit condemnation; the Prophetic report permits visiting graves because they remind people of the afterlife.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r4.claim: Because this hadith is not mutawatir, it cannot qualify, restrict, or abrogate the verse, but it can clarify what the verse leaves silent or general and reports an earlier prohibition.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r5.speaker: Râzî
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r5.claim: Razi reads the verse as divine astonishment: counting more dead has no benefit, while the proper purpose of visiting is softening the heart, loosening worldly attachment, and recalling the afterlife.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r6.speaker: Râzî
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r6.claim: Razi says the visitors did the reverse, approaching graves with hardened hearts and absorption in worldly love; the prophetic report calls grave visits a reminder.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r7.claim: The verse rebukes visits made to boast over the dead, not visits made for admonition and remembrance; the hadith establishes the latter's legitimacy.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r8.speaker: Âlûsî
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r8.claim: Alusi objects that the verse has no bearing on legitimate grave-visiting, then condemns ignorant visitors who boast over saints and commit other wrongs there.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#3/r9.claim: The author says Alusi's polemic risks making even reflective visits seem impermissible; Alusi likely meant the verse is silent on them, but should not have criticized the prior account of their legitimacy.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#4/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#4/r1.speaker: Ebû Hanîfe
ELMALILI:102:1-5#4/r1.claim: In advice to Abu Yusuf, Abu Hanifa counsels measured private correction of a ruler, debate with an heretical ruler through Quran and Sunnah, prayer for protection if rejected, remembrance of death, forgiveness for teachers, continued recitation, and frequent visits to graves, shaykhs, and blessed places.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r1.claim: Reports on grave visitation establish its legitimacy, wisdom, timing, method, and etiquette.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r10.claim: One benefits from the deceased by reflecting on their lives and works and keeping their good example alive.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r11.speaker: İbn Âbidîn
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r11.claim: Saints differ in their nearness to Allah, and visitors benefit in proportion to their own knowledge and insight into them.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r12.claim: A grave visit can affect a person like reading a book, awakening memories and reflection.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r13.claim: The best visit awakens the afterlife through tenderness of heart and sends the visitor back to life resolved to spend the remaining years in good works.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r14.claim: A hadith says grave visitation reminds people of the afterlife.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r15.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r15.claim: Visiting graves to boast and compete reverses their proper lesson and expresses extreme hardheartedness and heedlessness, prompting the rebuke of 102:1–2.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r16.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r16.claim: On a literal reading, competition may end when graves are visited, or grave visitation itself may end worldly greed.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r17.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r17.claim: Exegetes generally take grave visitation here as a metaphor for death, since death certainly ends competition.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r18.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r18.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r18.claim: Seeing a dead person, attending burial, or later visiting a grave can awaken reflection in receptive hearts, but this is not universal and is derivative of death.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r19.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r19.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r19.claim: If literal visitation were intended, the wording would encourage a required or recommended practice, conflicting with the following rebuke.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r2.claim: Visitation does not entail asking the dead for help or invoking them; visitors greet them and ask Allah for safety for living and dead alike.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r20.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r20.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r20.claim: The passage's purpose is to rebuke heedlessness and rivalry, not to promote grave visitation; this resolves the tension with the following prohibition.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r21.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r21.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r21.claim: The warning can mean that rivalry deludes people until their souls leave and their bodies enter the graves.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r22.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r22.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r22.claim: The rebuke warns people not to waste worldly life in rivalry; they will learn the gravity and outcome of their heedlessness later.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r3.claim: Visitors may recite Qur'an and dedicate its reward, while seeking Allah's will and preparing in complete faith for their own death.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r4.claim: The visit should prompt reflection on resurrection, judgment, the scales, and the destinations of deeds, strengthening resolve for faith and righteous action over rivalry and accumulation.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r5.claim: The dead have returned or been returned to Allah and enter their final states according to their standing before Him.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r6.claim: A prophetic report says a person will be resurrected with those he loves, so those who love the good join the good and those who love evil join the evil.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r7.claim: Love is valuable when it is for Allah and follows the command to follow the Prophet.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r8.claim: The dead have passed on: their deeds are theirs and yours are yours, so boasting or competing over them has no point.

ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:102:1-5#5/r9.claim: Worship and seeking aid belong to Allah; helping people for Allah is praised, while begging people is blameworthy, and asking the dead is especially unfitting.

QUTB-ZILAL:102:2/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:102:2/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:102:2/r1.claim: People leave behind what they competed over for a narrow grave, where there is no competition or boasting; they are urged to wake and look at where their distraction has brought them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p518/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p518/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p518/r3.claim: The surah rebukes neglect of Qur'anic evidence and Islam's call in favor of wealth, accumulation, and ancestral boasting until death, and warns against that course.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r1.claim: Hatta may mark the duration of distraction through a person's whole life, not the end of distraction followed by another activity, since all works cease at death.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r2.claim: On this reading, visiting graves means residing in them; “visit” hints that residence is temporary and people will leave them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r3.claim: The past tense “you visited” treats the future as already past because its occurrence is certain, as in “God's command came.”

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r4.claim: Alternatively, the endpoint is the object of rivalry: they compete over everything, even graves, as in the report about Banu Abd Manaf and Banu Sahm counting tombs.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r5.claim: The author cites al-Nabigha and a line attributed to Isam ibn Ubayd al-Zamani or Hammam al-Raqashi, where a grave stands for its occupant.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r6.claim: Al-maqabir is the plural of maqbara, pronounced with either fat-ha or damma on the b, and means land containing many graves.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p520/r7.claim: The rebuke is followed by afterlife warning: kalla deters and refutes their obsessive accumulation, sawfa guarantees the promised knowledge, and the omitted object is its evil outcome.

TABATABAI:102:1-6/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:102:1-6/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:102:1-6/r1.claim: The surah sharply rebukes people distracted by competing over wealth, children, and numbers, warning of loss and punishment and that they will be questioned about blessings they met with ingratitude.

TABATABAI:102:1-6/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:102:1-6/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:102:1-6/r2.claim: Raghib defines diversion as whatever occupies a person from what matters, and takathur as competing to have more wealth and prestige.

TABATABAI:102:1-6/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:102:1-6/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:102:1-6/r3.claim: Maqbara and maqbara both mean a burial place; visiting graves is a euphemism for death.

TABATABAI:102:1-6/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:102:1-6/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:102:1-6/r4.claim: The contextual meaning is that competition for worldly goods and adornment distracts from remembering God until death, leaving people heedless throughout life.

TABATABAI:102:1-6/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:102:1-6/r5.speaker: unnamed view
TABATABAI:102:1-6/r5.claim: Another interpretation has people boast about having more living men, then count and boast about their dead after all the living have died.

TABATABAI:102:1-6/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:102:1-6/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:102:1-6/r6.claim: The men-counting interpretation rests on reports that two Anṣar tribes first competed over the living and then the dead, or that Banu Abd Manaf and Banu Sahm did so in Mecca, prompting the surah.

TABATABAI:102:1-8/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:102:1-8/r3.speaker: قتادة
TABATABAI:102:1-8/r3.claim: A report says the surah concerned Jews boasting that their group outnumbered others; the rivalry kept them deluded until death.

ASAD-NOTES:102:1#n1/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:102:1#n1/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:102:1#n1/r1.claim: Takathur means greedily striving to increase benefits, whether tangible or intangible, real or illusory.

ASAD-NOTES:102:1#n1/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:102:1#n1/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:102:1#n1/r2.claim: Here it means obsessively seeking more comforts, material goods, and power over other people.

ASAD-NOTES:102:1/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:102:1/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:102:1/r1.claim: An exclusive pursuit of these gains blocks spiritual insight and acceptance of limits grounded in moral values.

ASAD-NOTES:102:1/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:102:1/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:102:1/r2.claim: The pursuit gradually destabilizes individuals and whole societies, eliminating their chance of happiness.

ASAD-NOTES:102:1/r3.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:102:1/r3.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:102:1/r3.claim: Unrestrained economic growth destroys the natural environment and brings frustration, unhappiness, and confusion to people losing their remaining spiritual orientation.

ASAD-NOTES:102:1/r4.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:102:1/r4.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:102:1/r4.claim: The unchecked pursuit of economic growth has brought frustration and confusion and threatens the remnants of spiritual and religious orientation.

ASAD-NOTES:102:intro/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:102:intro/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:102:intro/r1.claim: This early Meccan surah is a powerful prophetic passage about humanity's unbounded greed.

ASAD-NOTES:102:intro/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:102:intro/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:102:intro/r2.claim: It especially addresses greed-driven tendencies that have come to dominate technological societies.

BINTSHATI:v1p195/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p195/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p195/r1.claim: The Meccan surah is commonly dated as the sixteenth in revelation, after al-Kawthar; its concise, emphatic warning dominates its tone.

BINTSHATI:v1p195/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p195/r2.speaker: النيسابوري
BINTSHATI:v1p195/r2.claim: Al-Nīsābūrī links this surah to al-Qāriʿah; the author rejects a chronological link because Takāthur precedes it by thirteen surahs, while allowing a shared warning tone in the muṣḥaf arrangement.

BINTSHATI:v1p198/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p198/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p198/r3.claim: Ḥattā marks the endpoint: accumulation ends at the cemeteries, and the abrupt movement from rivalry to graves completes the warning.

BINTSHATI:v1p198/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p198/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p198/r4.claim: The Qur’an uses ziyārah only here and the related form tazāwar in al-Kahf; the root also denotes falsehood or deviation from truth.

BINTSHATI:v1p199/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p199/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p199/r1.claim: The sensory root of z-w-r is inclination or curvature; its derivatives describe turning toward someone, a dream-vision, or deviation from truth.

BINTSHATI:v1p199/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p199/r2.speaker: بعض المفسرين
BINTSHATI:v1p199/r2.claim: One interpretation takes the visit literally: people went to the graves to count their dead.

BINTSHATI:v1p199/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p199/r3.speaker: أبو حيان
BINTSHATI:v1p199/r3.claim: A second interpretation treats visiting as metaphorical mention of dead ancestors while boasting; Abū Ḥayyān rejects it because the wording visit is awkward for that sense.

BINTSHATI:v1p199/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p199/r4.speaker: بنو سهم وبنو عبد مناف
BINTSHATI:v1p199/r4.claim: A reported occasion says these clans competed over numbers, then counted their dead as well as the living after one claimed losses in pre-Islamic feuding.

BINTSHATI:v1p199/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p199/r5.speaker: الطبري
BINTSHATI:v1p199/r5.claim: A third interpretation takes visiting the graves as dying; al-Ṭabarī adopts it, citing familiar Arabic usage and poetry by Jarīr.

BINTSHATI:v1p200/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p200/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p200/r1.claim: Reading grave-visiting as death implies a temporary stay: visitors leave, so the wording itself hints at resurrection, reckoning, and recompense.

BINTSHATI:v1p200/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p200/r2.speaker: أعرابي
BINTSHATI:v1p200/r2.claim: A Bedouin who heard the verse inferred resurrection, saying visitors depart rather than remain.

BINTSHATI:v1p200/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p200/r3.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
BINTSHATI:v1p200/r3.claim: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz is also reported to have expressed a view like the Bedouin’s insight.

BINTSHATI:v1p200/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p200/r4.speaker: أبو حيان
BINTSHATI:v1p200/r4.claim: Abū Ḥayyān passes quickly over the Bedouin’s insight and instead cites a view that the verse rebukes boasting through repeated cemetery visits, distinguishing later permitted visits for admonition.

BINTSHATI:v1p200/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p200/r5.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p200/r5.claim: Al-Maqābir appears only in this verse, while qubūr appears five times and the singular qabr is used in al-Tawbah.

BINTSHATI:v1p201/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p201/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p201/r1.claim: Although maqābir suits takāthur in sound, its stronger reason is semantic: it evokes the vast collective cemetery across ages and classes, broader than individual graves.

BINTSHATI:v1p201/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p201/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p201/r2.claim: Reducing maqābir to a lexical synonym for graves misses its broad setting and the verse’s compressed journey from worldly rivalry to death.

CORPUSCORANICUM:102:2:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:102:2:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:102:2:anmerkung/r1.claim: The grave phrase most simply means until death or throughout one's life.

CORPUSCORANICUM:102:2:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:102:2:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:102:2:anmerkung/r2.claim: Tradition says Meccans counted dead relatives at graves to include them in rivalry for more; Paret treats the perfect as evidence of a past event, but the author favors a general statement and gnomic aspect.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p426/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p426/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p426/r1.claim: Islahi pairs al-Takāthur with al-Qāriʿah because both address what matters in the Hereafter.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p426/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p426/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p426/r2.claim: Al-Qāriʿah teaches that good deeds alone weigh in the Hereafter: more good deeds bring salvation, while greater evil brings lasting doom despite worldly treasure.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p426/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p426/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p426/r3.claim: This sūrah warns people who spend life competing for wealth and luxuries that they will face the dreadful consequences of forgetting accountability.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p428/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p428/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p428/r2.claim: Zurtum derives from a noun meaning simply to see, not the Urdu sense of a sacred visitation; here it means seeing the graves, or being consigned to them.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p428/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p428/r3.speaker: Ḥam āsī poet
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p428/r3.claim: A Ḥamāsī poem describes seeing one’s land after long absence and finding one’s friends gone while the land remains unchanged, illustrating the sense of visiting or seeing.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p428/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p428/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p428/r4.claim: Although Arabs kept and boasted of records of their dead, that custom is not what this verse means.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p428/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p428/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p428/r5.claim: The grave image preserves the rhyme and conveys pity for people who forfeited the Hereafter’s reward through endless rivalry for wealth.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:102:1/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:102:1/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:102:1/r5.claim: Maqabir is the plural of maqbara, meaning graves; commentators read “you visited the graves” metaphorically as dying while the contest continued, metaphorically as boasting over the dead, or literally as visiting graves to boast.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:102:1/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:102:1/r6.speaker: Müfessirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:102:1/r6.claim: Pre-Islamic Arabs boasted of abundant wealth, children, kin, and servants, then visited ancestors' graves to prove their tribe's superiority through its many notable dead.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:102:1/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:102:1/r7.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:102:1/r7.claim: Even if reports describe a specific occasion, the general target is human boasting in abundant wealth, offspring, and supporters; true superiority appears in the afterlife.

STUDYQURAN:102:2/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:102:2/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:102:2/r1.claim: The verse may refer to the clans' graveyard boasting, or to distraction continuing without repentance until people die.

STUDYQURAN:102:2/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:102:2/r2.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
STUDYQURAN:102:2/r2.claim: ʿAlī condemns graveyard visitors for drawing pride from ancestors' dead bodies and numbers instead of taking lessons that should inspire humility.

STUDYQURAN:102:intro/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:102:intro/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:102:intro/r1.claim: Most consider al-Takāthur Makkan and place it after al-Kawthar; a minority call it Madinan.

STUDYQURAN:102:intro/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:102:intro/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:102:intro/r3.claim: The best-attested occasion concerns Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū Sahm boasting about numbers, counting the living then dead; Sahm prevailed because it had more pre-Islamic dead.

STUDYQURAN:102:intro/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:102:intro/r4.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:102:intro/r4.claim: Others say the verses address the People of the Book, specifically the Jews of Madinah.

STUDYQURAN:102:intro/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:102:intro/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:102:intro/r5.claim: The first two verses expose delusion in accumulating worldly goods, a theme elsewhere in the Qur'an; vv. 3–8 warn persistent accumulators they will know Hellfire with certainty.
